name: The Great Camphor of Sugihokowakenomikoto Shrine

location.address: 154 Tanaka, Kawazu, Kamo District, Shizuoka 413-0504, Japan (grounds of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, also called Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine, behind and to the left of the main hall)
location.neighbourhood: Kawazu, on the east coast of the Izu Peninsula, roughly 19 km (about 35 rail km on the winding coastal Izu Kyuko Line) from Ito, which we already publish; the rail distance and journey time make this a separate trip rather than a day extension of Ito, so treated as its own single-tree place

access: Free. Shrine grounds, open to visitors. A sign at the entrance points visitors past two smaller camphors near the torii and the main hall to the real monument tree further in ('the natural monument great camphor is further on').
transport: Izu Kyuko Line to Kawazu Station, then about 12-15 minutes on foot (or a short bus ride from the station to the Kinomiyaguchi stop).
story:
Six of the seven are gone. Old Kawazu district was known for the Kawazu-go Nanakakae Nanakusu, its seven great camphors, and by the middle of the Meiji era this was the only one left standing.

It is not the first camphor you meet. Two smaller ones grow near the torii of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, the shrine locals call Kinomiya, and enough visitors have stopped at those that the shrine put up a sign telling them the natural monument is further on. It stands behind and to the left of the main hall: fifteen metres round, twenty-four metres tall, tied for the second-thickest tree in Shizuoka prefecture behind the camphor at Atami.

Published sources put it at a thousand years or more, which in Japan usually means tradition rather than a ring count, and this is no exception. The trunk can be measured, and has been twice. The Environment Ministry's giant-tree survey recorded fourteen metres of girth in 1990 and fifteen in 2001, ranking it nineteenth in the country and then thirty-second. The tree did not shrink; surveyors kept finding giants elsewhere.

Its two famous neighbours on the peninsula, at Atami and at Ito's Kuzumi-jinja, have both hollowed out. This one has not. It has dropped some large branches over the centuries and kept its trunk whole, which at this age and this girth is rare.

A national Natural Monument since December 1936.

name: The Weeping Akashide of Sajigami Shrine
age_estimate: disputed: traditionally said 700 years, town's own 2011 growth-ring study says 180-200 years

location.address: 2129 Ogunino, Hinode, Nishitama District, Tokyo, Japan (grounds of Sajigami-jinja, beside the approach path near the shrine entrance)
location.neighbourhood: Hinode, a town in the hills of western Tokyo; nearest place we publish is 38.8 km away, so treated as its own single-tree place

access: Free, shrine grounds. Viewable from the approach path; a fence protects the tree itself and the town's own guide states visitors may not touch it or step inside the fence without special permission.
transport: JR Itsukaichi Line to Musashi-Itsukaichi Station, then Nishi-Tokyo Bus toward Fussa Station, alight at the Sachikami stop; or about 10 minutes by car from the station.
story:
Every weeping akashide in Japan is a graft taken from this one tree. Akashide, the red-vein hornbeam, grows all over the country; a weeping form of it has turned up in the wild exactly once, here, beside the approach path of Sajigami-jinja in the hills of western Tokyo. The others, a few elsewhere in Hinode, one in Fussa, one in Tochigi that died in 1933, are all descended from this trunk by a difficult grafting technique, because seedlings and cuttings come up ordinary and upright.

Local tradition says it was carried from Yamashiro province when the shrine was founded, seven hundred years ago. The town's own science says no. Between 2008 and 2011 Hinode ran a vigour-recovery survey with tree doctors and observers from the Agency for Cultural Affairs. They counted about 150 rings in a dead limb, compared a girth of 135 centimetres recorded in 1939 with 198 centimetres in 2010, and put the tree at roughly 180 to 200 years. No akashide anywhere is known to live near seven centuries, and the town says plainly that the older figure has no clear basis.

It has been a national Natural Monument since August 1942, and as of 2013 the only one in Japan from the entire birch family. It is also six metres tall and easy to walk past. In 2010 the town felled 33 neighbouring trees to give it its light back.

name: The Kubo-zakura of Isazawa
species: Edo-higan Cherry (Cerasus itosakura, syn. Prunus itosakura / P. spachiana f. ascendens)
age_estimate: traditionally said to be about 1200 years

location.address: Kami-Isazawa, Nagai, Yamagata 993-0021, Japan (beside Isazawa Elementary School, western Nagai)
location.neighbourhood: Nagai, a city in the Okitama region of Yamagata Prefecture; nearest place we publish is 48.5 km away, so treated as its own single-tree place

access: Free. Public natural monument with its own free parking (17 spaces, 7 for tour buses); extra temporary parking is opened during the blossom festival.
transport: About 10 minutes by taxi from Yamagata Railway (Flower Nagai Line) Nagai Station; about 20 minutes by car from the Nanyo-Takahashi interchange of the Tohoku Chuo Expressway.
story:
Someone sheltering in the hollow at its base lit a cooking fire, and the Kubo-zakura lost two of its main limbs to it. That was the nineteenth century. The burn reshaped the crown into what now reads as two trees fused at the foot, and the tree has leaned on props ever since. More than sixty of them hold it up today.

It is one of the largest Edo-higan cherries in Tohoku: 13.85 metres tall, 8.1 metres round the trunk, 10.8 at the root collar, and a national Natural Monument since December 1924. An older nickname, Yontan-zakura, remembers a canopy said to have spread across roughly forty ares.

The legends are worth telling as legends. A 1925 prefectural survey recorded that the shogun Sakanoue no Tamuramaro planted it on the grave of Otama of the Kubo clan, who died of grief when his campaign moved on; other local versions credit a grieving lord. Both are stories, and so is the traditional age of 1,200 years. What is on record is that the lord of Yonezawa came to watch it bloom in the 1830s and 40s, and that the ten-are plot beneath it paid no tax until the Meiji Restoration.

Burnt heartwood cannot grow the fresh roots an old cherry uses to renew itself, so since 2006 conservators have packed peat moss and charcoal around the wound. By 2010 new roots up to three centimetres thick had reached the ground.

best_time.label: late April, when it blooms and the festival lights it after dark
